newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France aims for deficit below 3.0 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France aims for deficit below 3.0 pct of GDP.

text.p: France's conservative government on Wednesday approved a budget for next year designed to cut the public deficit to below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and smooth the way towards European monetary union.

Government officials said the budget contained a mix of tax and spending cuts designed to revive flagging consumer spending and economic growth while also ensuring France meets Maastricht Treaty conditions for joining a single European currency.
Next year is the crucial year for deciding which nations will be eligible, based on their fiscal and economic performances, to join a single currency in 1999.
"The effort to control spending will allow the deficit of all public bodies to remain below three percent of GDP," a statement released after a cabinet meeting said.
"In two and a half years, the deficit will have been reduced from nearly six percent to three percent of GDP," it added.

To reach that goal, the government was expected to announce spending cuts on job creation programmes and housing subsidies, while also using some creative accounting to bring the total deficit down from a goal of four percent of GDP this year.
In particular, the government said its targetted three percent deficit/GDP ratio took account of a one-off cash transfer from France Telecom to the state next year to cover pension liabilities.

But the government appeared to have shied away from the tough austerity expected earlier in the year, announcing that it would make only a small reduction in the central government budget deficit next year.

The statement said the central government budget deficit would be reduced to 283.7 billion francs ($55.07 billion) next year from 288 billion francs forecast for this year, after taking account of promised income tax cuts.
Economists said they were disappointed France had not gone for tougher spending curbs, particularly since Germany appeared to be trying to make real lasting cuts in public spending.
"It's quite disappointing, this smaller-than-expected cut in the central government budget deficit," JP Morgan economist David Naude said.
"My worry is it looks possible there will be a quality gap between the German and French fiscal packages," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.

With many details of the budget leaked in advance, the only real surprise was an announcement that the government would allow early withdrawals from popular savings schemes (PEPs), which it hoped would release about 15 billion francs for additional consumer spending.

It was also expected to announce later on Wednesday increases in excise duties on alcohol and tobacco which will help reduce the deficit on the welfare system, which is run separately from the central government budget.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said he expected the welfare system, which uses payroll taxes to fund healthcare, pensions and family benefits, to show a deficit of around 30 billion francs next year. ($1=5.151 French Franc)
